📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, homeowners have spent the past several years holding onto low-rate first mortgages while looking for ways to access their accumulated home equity.
  • Sources indicate that according to a recent analysis from Benutech that examined county-level mortgage recording data, more than 6 million second mortgages, including home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and closed-end second liens, were recorded between Jan.
  • It has been revealed that annual second-mortgage volume peaked in 2025 at 1.54 million loans, up 21.3% from 2024 and 32.4% from 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, homeowners have spent the past several years holding onto low-rate first mortgages while looking for ways to access their accumulated home equity. As rates have stayed above pandemic-era lows, the lock-in effect has helped sustain demand for home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and second mortgages and is expected to continue into 2027.

Sources indicate that according to a recent analysis from Benutech that examined county-level mortgage recording data, more than 6 million second mortgages, including home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and closed-end second liens, were recorded between Jan. 1, 2022, and Oct. 10, 2026.

It has been revealed that annual second-mortgage volume peaked in 2025 at 1.54 million loans, up 21.3% from 2024 and 32.4% from 2022. Through Oct. 10, 2026, 953,185 loans had been recorded, putting the market on pace for approximately 1.23 million loans for the year, the analysis found.

In October, a report from First American Data & Analytics found that U.S. homeowners held $13.2 trillion in accessible home equity in Q2 2026. Roughly 88% of that equity was tied to mortgages with rates below the market average.

Recent findings suggest that the Federal Reserve Bank of Latest York’s Center for Microeconomic Data reported similar findings in its quarterly report on household debt and credit, released at the start of November. HELOC balances increased by $23 billion to $481 billion, marking the largest quarterly increase since 2005. HELOC limits also rose by $31 billion, extending an expansion that began in 2022.

Industry observers note that as a result, the news cycle is abuzz with tales of borrowers turning to home equity products. But Anthony Stratis, vice president of lending partnerships at Figure, pointed out that demand has been building for several years, with homeowners using second liens to fund renovations and consolidate debt.

A significant share of Figure borrowers use home equity financing for those purposes, he said.

Stratis said the demand could outlast the current interest-rate environment as lenders improve their products and borrowers become more accustomed to using home equity to access cash.

In a recent development, “Home equity has really evolved to the point where it’s a pretty quick way to access cash when you need it for a project or whatever it might be,” Stratis stated. “I think that part is going to stay in place, and home equity is likely to have a place in the mortgage ecosystem for a while, independent of rates.”.

It has been revealed that matt Kroon, a home loan specialist at Churchill Mortgage, pointed out the “emotional connection” that borrowers have with their low, COVID-era mortgage rates. But persistently high rates and an aging home stock have led borrowers to inquire about other solutions.

Industry observers note that “Since affordability is a major concern right now, people are accessing their equity to make those improvements, or to pay off any higher-interest debt,” Kroon said. “Renovations and debt consolidation HELOCs are the main uses right now. However, some other uses include major expenses like a fresh roof, siding, furnace, etc.”.

According to recent reports, tom Hutchens, president of Angel Oak Mortgage Solutions, agreed with Stratis that his firm has seen steady HELOC demand over the past several years. Angel Oak, a non-QM lender, sees most of its demand among self-employed borrowers and those who use bank statement documentation to qualify for both first mortgages and HELOCs.

In a recent development, hutchens stated borrowers are also using home equity to pay down high-interest credit card balances. Angel Oak’s average combined loan-to-value ratio on HELOCs is in the 60% range, he said.

“Private capital is getting into the HELOC business. You’re going to start to see more and more HELOC securitizations,” he added.

Kevin Leibowitz, founder of Grayton Mortgage, noted that while HELOC inquiries have increased, not all conversations result in second mortgages.

Industry observers note that “[There is] lots of interest in HELOCs, a lot of production in HELOCs,” Leibowitz said. “But a lot of my conversations start with HELOCs, and we kind of pivot into other types of lending because the other types of lending might make sense.”.

The decision often comes down to comparing the cost of a borrower’s existing debt with the rate available on a new loan, he said. While borrowers may be reluctant to refinance a low-rate first mortgage, high-interest credit card balances and other obligations can make a new first mortgage more advantageous.

Benjamin Cohen, managing director and SVP of mortgage lending at Rate, noted borrowers who might have done a cash-out refinance in the past are now looking at a HELOC or a fixed-rate second mortgage like our HELoan.

In a recent development, “The math is pretty straightforward. If you owe $500,000 at 3% and need another $75,000, a cash-out refinance puts the entire $575,000 at today’s rate,” Cohen noted. “With a second mortgage, you keep the $500,000 at 3% and pay the new rate only on the $75,000. Even if the second mortgage carries a higher rate than the cash-out refinance, your blended rate across both loans can still be meaningfully lower. That can be a good compromise if the payments, fees and repayment terms make sense for you.”.

Sources indicate that leibowitz cited one borrower who had accumulated significant credit card debt after being laid off. By replacing the borrower’s first and second mortgages along with the credit card debt, he said, he improved the borrower’s monthly cash flow by about $3,500.

In a recent development, for borrowers with relatively low first-mortgage rates, keeping that loan and adding a HELOC may still be the better option. But HELOCs typically carry variable rates tied to the Wall Street Journal prime rate, exposing borrowers to higher payments if rates rise, Leibowitz remarked.

Adam Hopson, chief operating officer of Flyhomes, remarked home equity can also help homeowners purchase another property before selling their current one. However, the additional borrowing can affect their ability to qualify for a fresh mortgage.

It has been revealed that “A HELOC can unlock a down payment without unlocking a move,” Hopson mentioned. “Having access to equity and qualifying for the next mortgage are two different things, though.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that campbell, 64, who operates Extreme Realty Associates Inc.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bronx real estate broker Marcia Campbell was arrested and indicted for allegedly failing to disclose felony convictions and pending criminal charges when she applied to renew her Fresh York real estate broker license, New York Attorney General Letitia James announced Thursday.

Recent findings suggest that campbell, 64, who operates Extreme Realty Associates Inc. in the Bronx, is accused of falsely stating on a June 2026 renewal application that she had not been convicted of a crime and had no criminal charges pending since her previous renewal, according to the announcement from the Office of the Attorney General (OAG).

State regulators say that during that June 14, 2024, to June 13, 2026, period, Campbell had in fact pleaded guilty to two felonies in Westchester County and was facing 18 pending charges in Bronx County tied to alleged deed theft and real estate investment scams. Once the Upcoming York Department of State (DOS) discovered the alleged false statements, her broker license was administratively suspended.

Recent findings suggest that the case underscores how aggressively Upcoming York regulators and prosecutors are now scrutinizing license applications and renewals for real estate professionals, particularly in deed theft and fraud matters. For brokers and agents, the case is a reminder that criminal history disclosures on licensing forms are not procedural formalities, but sworn statements that can carry separate felony exposure if falsified.

The new indictment builds on a series of criminal matters involving Campbell in multiple counties.

In October 2024, Attorney General James and Bronx District Attorney Darcel Clark announced two separate indictments against Campbell. In the first, she and her co-conspirators — including her husband — were charged in an alleged deed theft scheme involving the childhood home of a Bronx woman. Prosecutors say the group gained the homeowner’s trust, then used fraudulent contracts bearing the homeowner’s forged signature to transfer the property to a shell tech giant they controlled and to obtain a $493,500 mortgage on the home. Campbell is scheduled to go to trial in that case on Feb. 22, 2027.

The second Bronx indictment accused Campbell of running a series of real estate investment scams. According to prosecutors, she induced clients to send her funds for purported real estate transactions, then kept the money and refused to return most of it. Those alleged scams took more than $250,000 from vulnerable Newly introduced Yorkers, including first-time homebuyers, immigrants and a personal friend, the OAG noted. A trial date in those cases has not yet been set.

Recent findings suggest that separate Westchester County prosecutions led to criminal convictions. On Dec. 18, 2025, Campbell pleaded guilty in two cases to Falsifying Business Records in the First Degree and Repeated Failure to File Corporate Taxes, both class E felonies. Authorities said those cases involved an alleged deed theft scheme that targeted three Westchester homes and involved roughly $2 million in fraudulently obtained loans. Campbell was sentenced to time served in those matters.

Despite those developments, prosecutors say Campbell submitted a broker license renewal application to DOS in June 2026 covering the period from June 15, 2026, through June 13, 2028. On that application, she allegedly answered “no” to questions asking whether she had been convicted of a crime or had criminal charges pending during the prior licensing period.

Attorney General James alleges Campbell knowingly omitted her December 2025 felony convictions in Westchester County and the 18 Bronx County charges that were already pending at the time she filed the renewal. When DOS identified the discrepancies and referred the matter to law enforcement, the agency suspended Campbell’s license.

It has been revealed that for brokerages, the case highlights the operational risk of failing to monitor the criminal and regulatory status of principal brokers and associated licensees. A suspended or revoked license can jeopardize transactions, commissions and firm reputation, especially in markets where deed theft has drawn heightened scrutiny from lawmakers and regulators.

Sources indicate that upcoming York officials at the state and local level have invested significant resources into deed theft enforcement in recent years, particularly in New York City and surrounding counties where equity-rich but cash-poor homeowners are frequent targets. These schemes often rely on trusted intermediaries, including licensed real estate professionals, to gain access to property records and homeowners.

“Upcoming Yorkers depend on real estate brokers to help them make some of the most crucial purchases of their lives,” Attorney General James remarked in the announcement, adding that Campbell allegedly abused her role “to steal New Yorkers’ homes and savings, then tried to hide her crimes to maintain her license.”.

For compliance officers at brokerages and franchisors, the case signals that state regulators are willing to cross-check licensing records with court and tax data and to bring independent criminal charges based solely on false or incomplete filings. Firms may want to revisit internal policies requiring prompt disclosure of arrests and convictions by licensed personnel and procedures for verifying those disclosures.

UPDATED 19:21 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

AI operational readiness requires more than selecting the right servers, storage and computing capacity.

Those considerations are particularly consequential for financial institutions, where reliability, regulatory obligations and the need to demonstrate returns on technology investments shape deployment decisions. Meanwhile, AI is changing the threat landscape, giving less sophisticated attackers access to capabilities that once required considerably greater resources, according to John Scimone, president and chief security officer of Dell Technologies Inc.

Sources indicate that “I think the pyramid still exists, but undoubtedly, the cost of entry and the barriers to entry have crumbled,” he told theCUBE. “Remarked another way, the least sophisticated attack tomorrow is more sophisticated than the world will have ever seen a year ago.”.

Scimone spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante during the Dell Technologies New York Symposium, part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exclusive coverage on theCUBE. Across the event, Dell executives and cloud infrastructure providers examined the economics of enterprise AI, the operational challenges of scaling infrastructure and the decisions shaping AI adoption.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with John Scimone:.

Here are three insights you might have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Dell Technologies Latest York Symposium:.

Dell has spent nearly two years running fully autonomous agents internally, capturing institutional knowledge in machine-readable skill files that guide their behavior. The effort is part of a broader reorganization of work around AI agents, according to John Roese, global chief technology officer and chief AI officer of Dell.

“It doesn’t mean you can’t use frontier models and open models,” he said during the event. “It just means that when you design your AI system, you need to realize that the thing that is your moat is not the actual tools. It’s not even the models. It’s the special knowledge that’s now manifesting in these upcoming forms that really capture what you know and do differently than your competitors.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with John Roese:.

It has been revealed that the financial side of AI operational readiness presents a different challenge. As enterprises scale their deployments, finance teams are establishing dedicated budget lines for token consumption and evaluating which workloads can run more economically on-premises. Repetitive financial processes, for example, can use open-weight models to convert variable token expenses into more predictable fixed costs, according to David Kennedy, chief financial officer of Dell.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s not necessarily about the amount and the cost of a token,” he told theCUBE. “It’s about the tokens you use. Can you be efficient with them? If you are, you’re going to see great outcomes.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with David Kennedy:.

Sources indicate that the growth of AI inference is changing how enterprises distribute workloads across cloud environments, data centers and edge devices. Dell’s expanded agentic AI portfolio reflects that shift, with solutions spanning desktop systems and data center infrastructure. Organizations are evaluating where to run models based on performance, data control and cost, according to Kyle Dufresne, senior vice president of sales at Dell.

Sources indicate that “We’re seeing the business owners saying, ‘Oh my gosh, these costs are getting really high for inferencing. How do we reduce those costs without curbing innovation?’” he stated during the event. “We’re finding it’s happening across that continuum but more and more right out at the far edge.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Kyle Dufresne:.

Infrastructure availability presents another challenge. Demand for AI servers has strained supplies of components ranging from memory and processors to rack-level cooling, networking and power equipment, according to David Schmoock, senior vice president of global revenue operations at Dell.

“We didn’t do that collaborative planning, and now your project may have been delayed 60, 90, 120 days, which has both the cost impact and a business impact,” he told theCUBE. “I would say bring us in earlier. Allow us to do that collaboration with you. I think, at the end of the day, you get the most optimal outcome.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with David Schmoock:.

In a recent development, AI operational readiness is also becoming a consideration for smaller businesses that need access to GPU computing without the resources of large enterprises. Comet Cloud Inc. is targeting this underserved market, where access to AI infrastructure can be constrained by purchasing commitments and provider priorities, according to Thomas Kato, founder and chief executive officer of Comet Cloud.

Industry observers note that “You go to [Amazon Web Services] now; they want a multiyear contract from you. They’re picking who they’re taking,” he said during the event. “To the small and medium businesses, they’re not even coming up on that scope at all to be able to have that AI. Really, that’s our focus.”.

Comet Cloud is developing an alternative approach aimed at giving smaller organizations greater control over their computing environments, Kato noted.

“What we do is we put together clusters, and we’re giving clusters to a whole organization. All their information, all their security, everything is within that cluster. There’s no one else tied or connected to it,” he told theCUBE.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Thomas Kato:.

Sources indicate that alpha Compute Corp. is also building its neocloud infrastructure around data sovereignty and confidential computing requirements. The tech giant’s sovereign-by-design approach is intended to help customers maintain control over sensitive workloads and meet data residency obligations, including those associated with European regulations, according to Tom Richer, executive vice president of Alpha Compute.

Recent findings suggest that “We start with the hardware. Think of a stack. All the way down to the chip level, we are creating enclaves,” he told theCUBE. “We’re a Dell partner, so we use Dell technology as well as Intel technology.”.

Industry observers note that keeping GPU infrastructure operational presents a different challenge for neocloud providers. Alpha Compute provides integrated infrastructure support and ongoing managed services to address those demands, Richer noted.

Sources indicate that “You can cobble together a lot of different providers, but then when stuff goes wrong, the finger-pointing starts,” he mentioned during the event. “You just want that integrated solution provider who can ensure success, help you with all of the build-out, then all of the … managed services to keep it going healthy and to keep everything performing in line with [service-level agreements].”.

Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse believes the recent crypto market sell-off stems largely from investors rotating capital into high-profile initial public offerings. The Ripple boss and crypto billionaire anticipates a recovery once Anthropic’s massive listing is fully absorbed.

Speaking to CNBC on November 19th, Garlinghouse drew a direct parallel to SpaceX’s public debut earlier in the year. He explained that when major IPOs generate intense demand, investors often sell liquid assets such as Bitcoin and XRP to free up cash for share subscriptions.

According to recent reports, the same pattern, he noted, unfolded ahead of Anthropic’s offering. After SpaceX completed its listing, crypto markets staged a notable rebound. Garlinghouse expects a similar bounce this time.

Anthropic, the artificial-intelligence manufacturer behind the Claude chatbot family, has priced its IPO at $83 per share, above the previously marketed range of $70 to $78.

The deal ranks among the largest IPOs in history, raising tens of billions of dollars and valuing the company in the trillion-dollar range, and shares are set to begin trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.

Such blockbuster offerings typically attract enormous institutional and retail interest, temporarily diverting capital from other risk assets. Once the primary allocation is complete and secondary-market trading stabilizes, some of that capital often flows back into crypto and other liquid markets.

Bitcoin had slipped near $62,000 on Wednesday before recovering above $63,000 early Thursday. Garlinghouse framed the dip as a temporary capital-rotation effect rather than a fundamental loss of confidence in digital assets. He also expressed confidence that Anthropic’s shares would trade strongly given the strong demand and pricing above the range.

Sources indicate that looking further ahead, Garlinghouse remained optimistic about blockchain’s long-term role. He predicted that within roughly a decade, blockchain technology will be deeply embedded across global financial infrastructure, much as artificial intelligence has already transformed multiple industries.

His comments highlight how large technology IPOs can create short-term pressure on crypto while potentially reinforcing longer-term narratives around innovation and capital markets.

webAI Releases TwIL-8B: A 5 GiB Open-Weight Reasoning Model With a 98.2 MATH-500 Score

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1077 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and states it tops Gemma 4 31B.
  • A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500.
  • webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and states it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

According to recent reports, the card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It states TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight users want to hear.

On MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

Sources indicate that the card is also more candid than most. It indicates TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

Here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

Gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

It has been revealed that none of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

Industry observers note that read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

Sources indicate that the AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card claims AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

In a recent development, against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card shows the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

The card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a major generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 newly introduced tokens and a 40,960-token context.

According to recent reports, anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card says all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

It has been revealed that the card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

Industry observers note that overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

It has been revealed that the useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meredith Wimbrow is leaving her role as director of stakeholder relations at the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) after about 20 months to become a vice president at Federal Hall Policy Advisors, she told HousingWire.

Wimbrow, a former FHFA Director Bill Pulte aide, is joining the private sector. POLITICO first reported on her transition. FHFA did not immediately respond to a request for comments.

According to recent reports, “I had a great experience at FHFA. It gave me firsthand understanding of the housing finance system and the policy making process, and the importance of the relationship between the government and the agency,” Wimbrow mentioned. “My role there was stakeholder relations. So I had a great opportunity to engage with the industry and work with folks in the housing space.”.

During her tenure, Wimbrow mentioned key discussions with industry participants focused on affordability, credit score modernization, oversight of the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) and the future of the housing finance system, as well as insurance modernization.

“The industry was very positive with the engagement, and they appreciated the focus of making housing affordable,” she said.

Wimbrow framed the career move as a natural shift from public service to advisory work.

Recent findings suggest that “I wanted to take what I learned on the agency side, particularly in stakeholder relations and industry engagement, and apply that experience in the private sector,” Wimbrow remarked. “It’s a natural step for me to decide on Fed Hall; they lobbied me, and they’re the best in the business.”.

Before joining FHFA, Wimbrow spent three years at the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), most recently as director of Build-PAC, NAHB’s bipartisan political arm focused on federal campaigns.

A 2022 study by researchers from the University of Sussex estimated that breaking Bitcoin's encryption within a day would require around 13 million physical qubits.

IBM Quantum Nighthawk, which IBM calls its fastest quantum processor, has 120 qubits. According to Nvidia, errors in quantum processors "limit the complexity and duration of the computations they can perform.".

Sources indicate that in 2024, Bitcoin developer Hunter Beast proposed BIP-360, a latest output type that would protect coins from quantum attacks. In July 2025, Casa co-founder Jameson Lopp also suggested a plan to phase out legacy signatures and move coins to quantum-resistant addresses.

Early coins mined by Satoshi Nakamoto sit on addresses with public keys that are already visible on the blockchain.

In November 2024, NIST proposed to stop allowing vulnerable public-key algorithms, including elliptic curve cryptography, after 2035.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lionel Fermin examines when growing businesses may need technology leadership for planning, security, spending, and long-term technology decisions.

HOBBS, N.M., Nov. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- When does a business need a Fractional CIO? A HelloNation article featuring insights from Managed IT Expert Lionel Fermin of GlobaTech Solutions in Hobbs, Fresh Mexico, explains when businesses may benefit from experienced technology leadership.

The HelloNation article explains that technology decisions often become more complicated as a business grows. Latest employees, software, equipment, and security risks can create challenges that basic technical support may not address. At that point, business leaders may need broader guidance about how technology supports the organization.

Sources indicate that the article describes a Fractional CIO as someone who provides technology leadership without serving as a full-time executive. While technical support typically focuses on fixing problems and keeping systems working, this role considers how technology decisions affect employees, customers, security, costs, and future business needs.

It has been revealed that this broader perspective can become key when several technology projects compete for attention. The article notes that businesses may recognize the need for improvements without knowing which ones should come first. Fractional CIO services can help prioritize projects according to risk, cost, and business value.

Technology planning is another major part of the role. Instead of waiting for systems or equipment to fail, the article explains that companies can prepare for equipment replacements, software changes, security improvements, and growth. Identifying major expenses early can also give leaders more time to compare options and prepare budgets.

Cybersecurity can create another need for technology leadership. The article notes that a security incident can interrupt operations, create financial losses, and affect customer relationships. Executive technology guidance can help leaders understand cybersecurity risks in business terms and determine which concerns deserve the most attention.

Sources indicate that the article also describes how Fractional CIO services can assist with customer or industry security requirements. Businesses may receive questionnaires or requests to demonstrate specific protections. Technology leadership can help identify gaps, organize responses, and provide a clearer view of existing security practices.

In a recent development, growth can also signal the need for more structured technology guidance. Systems that worked for a small team may become strained as a firm adds employees. The article explains that a technology strategy can help businesses prepare for greater demands on software, networks, security, and employee access.

Recent findings suggest that vendor management is another area where stronger oversight may be useful. Companies often work with separate providers for software, internet service, phones, security, and technical support. The article notes that reviewing vendor costs, contracts, performance, and responsibilities can help reduce duplication and clarify who handles notable technology needs.

Major business changes can also increase the need for planning. Opening a new office, replacing software, or hiring many employees may require coordination among leadership, employees, vendors, and technical teams. Managed IT Expert Lionel Fermin's insights featured in the article address how technology leadership can help keep these decisions connected to broader firm goals.

According to recent reports, the article notes that not every organization needs a full-time technology executive. Smaller businesses may instead need experienced guidance for certain projects or a limited number of hours. Warning signs can include rising technology costs, repeated cybersecurity concerns, unsuccessful projects, or leaders spending too much time managing technology questions.

According to recent reports, A lack of shared planning may provide another warning sign. When departments make separate technology decisions, businesses can face higher costs, security gaps, and software problems. The article explains that a shared technology strategy can provide clearer direction across the organization.

According to recent reports, ultimately, the article explains that the value of a Fractional CIO centers on planning and leadership rather than daily troubleshooting. Strong technology guidance can help businesses organize decisions about systems, security, spending, growth, and long-term needs.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Howard Hanna Real Estate Services is joining the growing roster of real estate firms facing a lawsuit over a “transaction fee” a consumer was allegedly forced to pay in conjunction with their real estate transaction.
  • Earlier this month, first-time homebuyer Dena Bergamasco filed a suit against Howard Hanna over a $395 “Realtor Transaction Fee” she claims she was charged on top of the buyer broker commission she paid related to her October 2021 home purchase.
  • Bergamasco is being represented by Kopelowitz Ostrow P.A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Howard Hanna Real Estate Services is joining the growing roster of real estate firms facing a lawsuit over a “transaction fee” a consumer was allegedly forced to pay in conjunction with their real estate transaction.

Earlier this month, first-time homebuyer Dena Bergamasco filed a suit against Howard Hanna over a $395 “Realtor Transaction Fee” she claims she was charged on top of the buyer broker commission she paid related to her October 2021 home purchase.

Bergamasco is being represented by Kopelowitz Ostrow P.A. one of the firms representing plaintiff Gregory Deivert in his transaction fee lawsuit filed against a Keller Williams franchise last month.

Attorneys for Bergamasco claim in the filing that as her buyer broker Howard Hanna breached its fiduciary duty and violated the state’s Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law in charging her this fee, which the suit describes as a “cash grab.”.

Bargamasco claims that the $395 fee was charged “for nothing” with “no service behind it, no cost behind it, and no name that accurately describes it.”.

“It is money taken from a client by the broker who was supposed to be looking out for her,” the complaint states.

According to the complaint, the fee was “wedged”  between third-party charges for a pest inspection fee and an owner’s title insurance premium in the closing disclosure. Additionally, the complaint alleges that the brokerage coaches agents to tell clients that the fee is mandatory and serves a “processing” or “administrative” purpose.

Sources indicate that in the filing, Bergamasco’s attorneys state that she paid $217,000 for her home, with $213,069 of this coming from a federally insured mortgage and $10,850 coming from a second loan from the Pennsylvania Housing Finance Agency. In addition to this, the sellers awarded her a $7,300 credit to use toward closing costs. In total, the filing states that Bergamasco brought $788.95 in cash to her closing, not even double the cost of the alleged fee. According to the filing, with the home purchase transaction occurring prior to the Sitzer/Burnett commission lawsuit settlement, the plaintiff’s buyer broker commission was paid by the home seller and that Bergamasco paid for the paperwork completed by the settlement agent and title insurance provider at the closing.

It has been revealed that the suit is seeking class action status and the plaintiff has demanded a jury trial. Bergamasco said she is seeking damages and a permanent injunction preventing Howard Hanna from charging this fee in the future.

Howard Hanna did not immediately return HousingWire’s request for comment regarding the lawsuit.

It has been revealed that the complaint claims that the practice of charging consumers a “transaction fee” is not unique to Howard Hanna. This is evidenced in the other lawsuits that have popped up this year, including the lawsuit against Keller Williams Elite over an alleged $650 “broker fee” and a since voluntarily dismissed lawsuit filed against Compass over an alleged $475 transaction fee.

Some reports, such as one from the Consumer Policy Center, claim that consumers pay up to $2 billion in brokerage transaction fees each year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elite university Harvard maintains significant Bitcoin exposure as it holds over 3 million shares of a Bitcoin ETF, a recent regulatory filing has revealed.

Harvard University remains highly exposed to Bitcoin (BTC) as the elite institution continues to hold over 3 million shares of a Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF).

As per Bitcoin Magazine’s Nov. 16 report, Harvard Management Tech giant, which manages Harvard University’s endowment, held 3,044,612 shares of BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) as of Sept. 30, 2026.

The Form 13F filing by Harvard University with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) showed that its investment in the Bitcoin ETF was worth roughly $144.1 million at the end of the third quarter.

Notably, Harvard did not change its Bitcoin ETF share count during the third quarter. The university held the same number of shares as reported at the end of June.

Harvard first disclosed its investment in BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF during the second quarter of 2025.

According to recent reports, as per Harvard's Form 13F filing submitted on Aug. 8, 2025, it held 1,906,000 IBIT shares at the end of the second quarter. The investment was worth roughly $116.7 million as of June 30.

The university subsequently increased its Bitcoin exposure significantly.

For instance, at the end of September 2025, Harvard held 6,813,612 IBIT shares, worth roughly $442.9 million. The Bitcoin ETF was the biggest investment that Harvard publicly reported at the time.

In a recent development, later, however, the university started trimming its Bitcoin exposure. For example, during the fourth quarter of 2025, Harvard reduced its IBIT holdings by about 21.4%. Its total share holdings fell to 5.35 million.

It has been revealed that during the first quarter of 2026, Harvard again reduced its Bitcoin exposure by 43.1%. This brought down the number of IBIT shares to roughly 3.04 million.

Since then, the university has maintained this number of shares. Harvard's quarter-end share count has remained unchanged in recent quarters.

Harvard University is not the only top-tier American university that has gained exposure to the biggest cryptocurrency by market capitalization.

Sources indicate that in October 2024, Emory University became the first U.S. university endowment to publicly disclose its holdings in a Bitcoin ETF.

It held roughly 2.7 million shares of Grayscale’s Bitcoin Mini Trust, worth over $15 million at the time.

Meanwhile, in May 2025, Brown University disclosed its holdings of 105,000 shares of BlackRock's IBIT, worth roughly $4.9 million as of March 31 of that year.

Later, Brown doubled its stake, bringing its holdings to 212,500 shares.

Meanwhile, Dartmouth College has also joined the list of universities with exposure to cryptocurrency ETFs.

Industry observers note that in its recent filing, Dartmouth College disclosed that it held 201,531 IBIT shares. The investment was worth roughly $9.5 million as of the end of September 2026.

Homebuilders’ $30B buying spree has cooled; now it’s all execution

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2807 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the better part of 15 years, U.S.
  • The buying continued through 2026, with Berkshire Hathaway‘s $8.5 billion acquisition of Taylor Morrison and Sumitomo Forestry‘s approximately $4.5 billion purchase of Tri Pointe Homes among the year’s largest deals.
  • Yet even as those transactions have reshaped the industry’s competitive landscape, the economics of homebuilding have shifted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the better part of 15 years, U.S. homebuilding has been on a mergers-and-acquisitions buying spree. Since 2010, more than 200 homebuilder transactions have conservatively totaled more than $30 billion in announced deal value, based on just seven of the largest acquisitions and excluding scores of private-tech giant transactions whose purchase prices were never disclosed.

The buying continued through 2026, with Berkshire Hathaway‘s $8.5 billion acquisition of Taylor Morrison and Sumitomo Forestry‘s approximately $4.5 billion purchase of Tri Pointe Homes among the year’s largest deals. More recent transactions included Daiwa House subsidiary Stanley Martin‘s July acquisition of Holiday Builders, Dream Finders Homes‘ August acquisition of Beazer Homes, and Century Communities’ October purchase of HistoryMaker Homes.

Yet even as those transactions have reshaped the industry’s competitive landscape, the economics of homebuilding have shifted. Weak demand, costly sales incentives, shrinking margins, and uncertainty over land and home values are forcing acquirers to reconsider not only which businesses are worth buying but also how the companies they already own should operate.

“We’re not busy now,” one deeply experienced homebuilding M&A dealmaker told me recently. “This is no time to be trying to take a seller to market for acquisition. Nothing’s happening.”.

That assessment does not mean homebuilding consolidation has ended. It’s still “morning time in America” for homebuilding’s inevitable grind toward concentration of fewer, ever larger, more industrialized homebuilding giants.

My source’s observation suggests that the economics of bringing newly introduced sellers to market have become harder, even as the largest and best-capitalized acquirers continue pursuing strategic combinations.

According to recent reports, business and investment models in homebuilding can look remarkably good when demand, prices, and asset values are rising. The real test comes when the cycle turns, gravity takes hold, and assumptions that worked on the way up begin to break down. That’s when the industry’s outliers distinguish themselves, not simply through stronger balance sheets, but by how well their people work together, how promptly they adapt their processes, how effectively they serve customers, and how consistently they outperform competitors when business conditions get messy.

It has been revealed that that is the test now confronting the companies assembled through homebuilding’s extraordinary consolidation era. Have their acquisitions produced merely bigger enterprises, or have they developed the leadership, operating discipline, local knowledge, and capacity to improve that will make them fundamentally better homebuilders with greater connectivity to and attainability for America’s economically bifurcated households?

According to recent reports, the answer will increasingly depend on what happens inside the enterprises they’ve acquired. The challenge is to capture the value of their land positions while developing the people, operating systems, technologies, and organizational capabilities needed to replenish those positions, improve profitability, and serve customers more efficiently in a difficult market likely to extend into 2027 and potentially 2028.

That is where the next, and perhaps most demanding, phase of homebuilding consolidation begins.

Homebuilding acquisitions are distinct from many other corporate combinations because the value of the acquired business is inseparable from its land positions and the people capable of turning those positions – sustainably and repeatedly – into profitable homes.

It has been revealed that an attractive acquisition may bring years of controlled lots, entitled development opportunities, established relationships with landowners and municipalities, and access to markets that would take an outsider years to enter. It may also include an experienced management team, trusted trade relationships, established brands and the organizational knowledge and local intel needed to perpetuate the business beyond its current land pipeline.

Those assets are related, but they are not interchangeable. When one goes missing, the others rapidly fall out of balance. The value of the land depends on its location, basis, development requirements, timing, and the demand for homes that can be built on it profitably. Realizing that value depends on decisions about product, construction costs, sales strategy, purchasing, development sequencing, and capital allocation.

An acquirer that buys a good land portfolio but loses the ability to develop and replenish it efficiently may find that the acquisition’s original promise was a mere blip. An acquirer that preserves an admired local management organization without improving its operating economics may find that the business remains well regarded yet increasingly uncompetitive.

Successful acquisitions require balancing those two realities. The objective is to capture the value of the acquired land and operating platform as a launching pad for building the leadership, relationships, systems, and financial discipline needed to extend that profitability long after the original inventory has been delivered.

That balance of 100% binding capabilities becomes harder to hold together when market conditions weaken.

For years, one of the most attractive features of selling to Berkshire Hathaway’s Clayton Properties Group or one of the major Japan-based acquirers was the prospect of continuity.

Many regional builders joined larger, well-capitalized ownership organizations while retaining key elements of their identities, management teams, local relationships, and operating independence. That approach appealed to owners seeking liquidity or a succession solution without losing the character of the companies they had built.

It also made strategic sense. Local knowledge, land relationships, management experience, customer trust, and an almost irreplicable entrepreneurial fire and come-what-may resiliency were among the assets the buyers sought to acquire.

In a recent development, but serving as a benevolent, deep-pocketed, and patient capital-access channel for a local autonomy confederation across an expanding collection of businesses comes at a cost. Separate purchasing organizations, technology systems, back-office functions, product-development practices, and management structures can limit the benefits of larger ownership. When sales are strong and margins are healthy, those costs may be easier to absorb. When sales slow, incentives rise, and profitability contracts, the economics become less forgiving.

In a recent development, the pressure to coordinate operations, consolidate functions, standardize selected processes, and reduce unnecessary overhead intensifies. So do difficult decisions about regional leadership, divisional responsibilities, and the roles of managers at the divisional and neighborhood level who helped make the acquired businesses successful in the first place.

In a recent development, those decisions can be disruptive, especially for employees and former owners who believed their companies would continue operating as they had before the acquisition and, in some cases, had enjoyed a solid few-year runway of exactly that. Some will regard the changes as evidence that the fresh parent does not understand the business it acquired. Others will see them as necessary steps toward strengthening the combined organization.

Eliminating management positions or consolidating administrative functions does not, by itself, demonstrate operational improvement. Nor does a departure from established practices necessarily indicate that an acquirer has made a strategic mistake or an unforced error.

Recent findings suggest that the relevant test is whether the changes improve the organization’s ability to develop land, build homes, serve customers, maintain valuable relationships and generate returns that stakeholders and owners can count on as durable. That is a more useful standard than judging an acquisition by how many legacy executives remain in place or by how many familiar operating practices survive.

An important distinction exists among the companies driving the latest phase of consolidation. Daiwa House, Sekisui House, Sumitomo Forestry, and Berkshire Hathaway operate with strategic planning horizons and ownership structures that can offer greater flexibility than the quarter-to-quarter performance pressures faced by many publicly traded U.S. homebuilders.

Recent findings suggest that the Japanese companies are publicly traded, and Berkshire Hathaway is accountable to its shareholders. None is insulated from financial performance requirements. But their diversified businesses, substantial resources, and long-term commitments to housing and related industries can allow them to invest in capabilities whose returns may take years to materialize.

So far, that difference has played out as an “acquirer-of-choice” factor as homebuilding firm sellers considered how firms organize and develop the businesses they acquire.

A longer-term ownership philosophy does not require codifying every management position or maintaining every regional operating structure indefinitely. In fact, patient capital may be most valuable when it enables an organization to undertake difficult transformations without expecting every investment to deliver an immediate earnings benefit.

The challenge is to distinguish costs that can be eliminated from capabilities that need strengthening.

Japan-based companies also have another potentially vital advantage. Their experience with industrialized construction, standardized components, manufacturing systems, production engineering and deeply vertical integration extends well beyond what is typical of conventional American site-built homebuilding.

Clayton also brings experience in manufactured housing, factory-based production, and vertically integrated housing-related businesses. Its expanding site-built platform, particularly following the Taylor Morrison acquisition, creates opportunities to combine capabilities that have historically operated in unrelated realms of the residential construction business.

None of this means that industrialized methods developed elsewhere can simply be transplanted into American site-built construction. Differences in building codes, product preferences, transportation, trade labor, land development, and construction practices remain unsolved obstacles.

The industry has not yet demonstrated that these capabilities can be deployed broadly enough to transform the economics of conventional site-built housing. Still, the long-term strategic opportunity is hard to refute.

A collection of independently operated regional builders can provide market presence, land access, local expertise and “trust capital.” A more coordinated enterprise may also provide the common systems, product architecture, production volumes, and organizational learning needed to adapt industrialized methods across multiple markets.

According to recent reports, as ambitions go, that’s far bigger than reducing SG&A. It also raises a question that applies to every major acquirer: Which capabilities should remain local, which should be shared across the enterprise, and which should be fundamentally reengineered into the holistic, interoperable system modern homebuilding organizations seem to need?

Homebuilding has long featured an argument over whether privately held regional builders are inherently better businesses than their larger public competitors. The case for private builders emphasizes their closeness to customers, knowledge of local land markets, relationships with municipalities and trades, and the loyalty and committed engagement of talented employees who have worked together for years.

In a recent development, those advantages are real in many companies. They can influence everything from land acquisition opportunities to construction execution and customer referrals. But private ownership does not guarantee those qualities, just as public or institutional ownership does not necessarily diminish them.

A privately held tech giant can become inefficient, undercapitalized, or resistant to change. A large enterprise can cultivate strong local leadership, build trusted community relationships, and adopt operating practices that improve the customer experience.

The more useful distinction concerns the quality of the operating organization, a characteristic we’ve talked about as homebuilding’s “outlier” factor.

Does it put decisions in the hands of people with the knowledge to make them? Does it give those people the resources, information, and accountability to perform effectively? Can it identify successful practices and extend their benefits beyond the division where they originated?

Answers to those questions reveal more than public or private ownership labels. They also help explain why the integration decisions now confronting the major consolidators are so difficult. An organization can destroy valuable local capabilities by centralizing too much. It can also waste substantial resources and miss opportunities to improve by centralizing too little.

Industry observers note that integration is knowing the difference. Some acquirers are good integrators. That doesn’t mean people swept up in them, or spat out due to them, agree.

For decades, scale in homebuilding has largely meant more closings, more communities, more controlled lots, greater geographic reach, and increased purchasing power that leads to market-share advantages. Those advantages remain as a bulwark of near-flywheel-like value creation. Larger builders can spread fixed costs across more homes, negotiate favorable supplier arrangements, diversify market exposure, and access capital on terms that smaller competitors may struggle to match.

Still, everyone who’s done well in the business can attest that size alone does not explain why some organizations consistently outperform others.

In a recent development, A more meaningful definition of scale includes an enterprise’s ability to combine capital, land, local knowledge, talent, technology, and relationships into an operating system that continuously improves performance. In that sense, homebuilding was AI before AI was cool because its best operators knew and practiced “recursive learning” as a core skill set.

That means acquiring land at bases that support acceptable returns under realistic demand assumptions. It also means developing products that customers value without unnecessary design, material, or construction complexity.

It means coordinating suppliers and trades to reduce delays, rework, and waste. It also means developing managers who can exercise sound judgment locally while drawing on the organization’s broader capabilities. It also means using information gathered across markets to make better decisions throughout the enterprise.

A builder operating in 20 markets should have opportunities to learn from 20 distinct sets of customers, land conditions, construction challenges, and operating practices. But those opportunities yield little advantage if the information remains trapped within individual divisions or if the organization lacks the discipline to identify and transfer improvements.

This is where AI-powered data systems and other technology capabilities could change the economics of scale. Better demand forecasting, more accurate construction scheduling, earlier detection of cost overruns, improved land underwriting, and more systematic comparisons of product performance could help organizations spot problems sooner and make decisions faster.

AI could help reveal patterns that managers would otherwise struggle to recognize in large volumes of operational data. It could also make institutional knowledge more accessible to those making daily decisions about land, purchasing, construction, and sales.

But value will not come from installing technology alone. Companies will need reliable data, consistent definitions, disciplined operating processes, and managers who can distinguish useful insights from misleading conclusions. They will also need to recognize that an approach that works in one market may be a fool’s errand in another.

Industry observers note that competitive advantage will belong to organizations that can repeatedly measure performance, understand what drives it, test improvements, and incorporate what they learn into their operating practices. That is how scale becomes a capability rather than merely a measurement of size.

Industry observers note that the difficult market conditions facing builders through 2027, and potentially into 2028, will make these distinctions more apparent. Management teams will face pressure to reduce overhead, preserve liquidity, reassess land commitments, control construction costs, and improve returns on capital. Some will need to reorganize divisions, consolidate functions, or change leadership.

According to recent reports, the companies that emerge stronger will not necessarily be the ones that make the deepest cuts. They will be the ones that understand which costs can be eliminated without harming the business and which investments are necessary to improve its future performance. That requires financial discipline, but it also requires patience, sound leadership judgment, and a willingness to challenge established practices.

It may require replacing an operating system that has worked adequately for years. It may also mean changing the responsibilities of respected executives or asking local teams to adopt practices developed elsewhere in the enterprise.

It has been revealed that it may also require resisting the temptation to standardize activities that rely on local relationships and judgment. The objective should be neither to preserve acquired companies exactly as they were nor to eliminate their differences in pursuit of corporate uniformity.

It should be to develop organizations that can achieve what their constituent businesses could not accomplish independently.

The returns earned by companies that participated in homebuilding’s consolidation era will not reflect the ultimate opportunity. American homebuilding remains a uniquely complex process of converting land, capital, materials, labor, knowledge, and time into a finished product that households can purchase. Every unnecessary delay, redundant process, avoidable error, excessive handoff, and poorly coordinated decision adds cost somewhere along that process.

Some of those costs are so sticky they seem almost unavoidable. Others reflect operating practices that have persisted through the decades because the industry has struggled to coordinate the many participants involved in building a home.

Larger enterprises with better information, stronger leadership, deeper technical capabilities, and greater capacity to invest in improvement can change that.

The goal should be a homebuilding value stream that produces more value with less wasted time, effort, and expense, i.e., less “stream.”.

Recent findings suggest that better execution will not, by itself, overcome high land prices, expensive financing, restrictive regulation, infrastructure constraints, or the gap between household incomes and housing costs. Those barriers remain substantial. But homebuilders have meaningful control over how they organize their businesses and how efficiently they turn resources into finished homes.

The industry’s era of consolidation has brought together an enormous collection of land assets, operating organizations, local relationships, and management talent under larger ownership platforms. What happens next will determine whether those combinations yield more than additional market share and purchasing leverage.

The most vital measure of homebuilding’s great acquisition era may ultimately have little to do with how many companies changed hands or how much their buyers paid.

It may be how much better those enterprises become at converting land, capital, talent, and knowledge into homes that more American households can afford.

Sources indicate that the CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

According to recent reports, A Monero token crashed 99% on Friday after 5.2 million XMR1 tokens moved from a wallet tied to its creator, triggering a massive sell-off on Hyperliquid. The token, issued through crypto swap service Wagyu, plunged from around $494 to below $1 in 35 minutes. The wallet receiving the tokens sold enough to generate $13.22 million in USDC before converting the proceeds into 7,467 ETH.

It has been revealed that wagyu’s wallet security and the backing behind its wrapped Monero product are being questioned. And the sell-off also sent shockwaves through the Monero market, although native XMR remained a separate asset from the collapsing XMR1 market.

🚨HYPERLIQUID WRAPPED MONERO APPEARS TO BE GETTING HACKED!@lookonchain flagged an attacker wallet that received 5.2 million $XMR1, dumped it on Hyperliquid, then used the proceeds to buy ethereum:native.So far the address has spent $13.22M USDC for 7,467 ethereum:native.… pic.twitter.com/boP1oXXmjl.

According to recent reports, the incident began this morning when the account responsible for deploying XMR1 transferred tokens to a newly created wallet. Blockchain intelligence firm Bitquery identified three separate transfers between 04:46 and 05:16 UTC. Two transactions moved 100,000 XMR1 each, followed by a much larger transfer of 5 million tokens.

The receiving wallet had been created that morning. It began selling shortly after receiving the tokens, overwhelming buyers on Hyperliquid’s order book. XMR1 had traded near $500 throughout the previous week. Its price then collapsed to $1 within 30 minutes, leaving holders with almost nothing.

Bitquery traced 363,804 tokens sold for $13.5 million. The remaining 4.83 million tokens stayed in the receiving wallet during its investigation. The sell-off also exposed how concentrated XMR1’s supply had been. Before the transfers, its deployer account still controlled 93% of the token’s supply.

Hyperliquid transfers require signatures from the account’s own key, rather than an ordinary trading API wallet. This means whoever authorized the transfers likely had access to the deployer’s main key. Whether someone stole that access or used it legitimately remains unknown.

Discover: The Best Token Presales.

The damage extended beyond traders watching XMR1 collapse on their screens. It matched the seller’s transactions against 388 accounts that purchased the dumped tokens. One buyer alone paid $3.56 million, while 27 large buyers accounted for 77% of the total proceeds.

Industry observers note that the wallet did not leave the money sitting in USDC. It began moving funds through Hyperliquid’s bridge into Arbitrum shortly after selling.

XMR1 hack: 388 Hyperliquid buyers paid $13.50 million for a token that fell 99.8%https://t.co/k5ggHcH6Al.

Industry observers note that on Arbitrum, the wallet exchanged $13.22 million in USDC for 7,467 ETH through CoW Protocol. It then routed much of the Ethereum through Socket, Mayan, and Stargate. 6,810 ETH then arrived on Ethereum after those bridge transactions. Approximately 4,836 ETH landed in a newly created wallet that had not sent any funds onward.

The investigation also identified 7,348 ETH across three wallets during its tracking window. That left a substantial amount of the proceeds sitting outside the original trading account.

According to recent reports, the incident has put Wagyu’s bridge infrastructure under scrutiny. XMR1 itself is Monero on Hyperliquid, but through Wagyu’s bridging service. People can move native XMR into the service and receive XMR1 for trading. They can also reverse the process to recover their Monero.

Native XMR did not suffer the same collapse. Monero continued trading around $470–$482, while XMR1 lost virtually all its market value.

Holders now face a difficult question: Can they still exchange their remaining XMR1 for native Monero?

Recent findings suggest that the incident also comes weeks after Wagyu disclosed a separate data leak on October 28. Researchers identified exposed records potentially linking crypto deposits, Monero receiving addresses, and customer IP addresses.

Industry observers note that wagyu previously stated customer funds remained unaffected by that incident. No established connection links the October leak to Friday’s wallet transfers.

In a recent development, the latest investigation also uncovered another potential concern. The same deployer account controls 99.97% of ZEC1, a separate token representing Zcash on Hyperliquid.

CrowdStrike reportedly in talks to acquire cybersecurity provider Zscaler

💡 Key Takeaways
  • is reportedly in talks to buy Zscaler Inc., a publicly traded provider of cybersecurity software.
  • Sources told Bloomberg today that the acquisition could “come together soon.” However, they cautioned that it’s still possible the talks will fall through.
  • Investors seem to be confident that the deal will materialize.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:50 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. is reportedly in talks to buy Zscaler Inc., a publicly traded provider of cybersecurity software.

Sources told Bloomberg today that the acquisition could “come together soon.” However, they cautioned that it’s still possible the talks will fall through.

Investors seem to be confident that the deal will materialize. Zscaler’s share price jumped more than 16% in after-hours trading, while CrowdStrike dropped about 4.8%.

Software buyouts tend to value the acquired company at a premium to its last unaffected market capitalization. As a result, CrowdStrike is likely to pay more than the $32 billion Zscaler was worth at the end of today’s trading session. That means the deal could take CrowdStrike’s market capitalization above $250 billion.

CrowdStrike sells one of the world’s most popular cybersecurity platforms. Falcon can detect and block malicious activity across cloud instances, on-premises servers, employee devices and other assets. It also automates certain related tasks, such as finding sensitive records that are stored in an insecure manner.

Zscaler competes in a different part of the cybersecurity market. It sells software that protects the network connections through which a manufacturer’s employees access its business applications.

It has been revealed that enterprises historically used virtual private network, or VPN, tools for that task. Such programs tend to be quite slow. More significantly, they give employees access to the entire corporate network rather than to the specific applications they need for their work. That broad access can create cybersecurity risks.

According to recent reports, zscaler sells a zero-trust network access, or ZTNA, platform designed to replace legacy VPN software. It limits the number of applications that workers can access within the corporate network. If Zscaler detects risky activity, it asks the affected user to complete additional authentication steps.

Recent findings suggest that the manufacturer’s ZTNA software doubles as an observability tool. Administrators can monitor employees’ connections for technical issues that may hinder productivity. A built-in artificial intelligence assistant, the ZDX Agent, generates troubleshooting advice.

Zscaler also competes in other product categories where CrowdStrike has a limited presence. Notably, it offers a tool that deploys bogus applications, user passwords and files in customer networks. Those simulated assets act as sensors. When an attempt is made to access one of them, Zscaler Deception notifies the customer that a cyberattack is underway.

The potential deal would mark CrowdStrike’s largest acquisition by a wide margin. The manufacturer’s biggest buyout to date is its $970 million purchase of startup SGNL Inc., which closed earlier this year. The deal bought CrowdStrike a platform that can automatically end consumers’ application sessions when it detects cybersecurity issues.

Ripple's Schwartz Reveals Why XRP Ledger Used Satoshi's Code

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ripple CTO emeritus David Schwartz has shared the reason the XRP Ledger (XRPL) used code and cryptography from Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, in its early stages.
  • 16 post on X, Schwartz noted they primarily chose to do so for security reasons and to prevent backlash from the Bitcoin community when the XRP Ledger was still in its early development.
  • The conversation started when prominent XRPL validator Vet (@Vet_X0) pointed out how some of Satoshi Nakamoto's initial design decisions are still present in the XRP Ledger's structure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ripple CTO emeritus David Schwartz has shared the reason the XRP Ledger (XRPL) used code and cryptography from Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, in its early stages.

In his Nov. 16 post on X, Schwartz noted they primarily chose to do so for security reasons and to prevent backlash from the Bitcoin community when the XRP Ledger was still in its early development.

The conversation started when prominent XRPL validator Vet (@Vet_X0) pointed out how some of Satoshi Nakamoto's initial design decisions are still present in the XRP Ledger's structure.

Vet remarked that the XRP Ledger initially used helper functions from the original Bitcoin software, including timekeeping functions coded by Satoshi Nakamoto himself.

Industry observers note that some of those helper functions were reportedly copied by Jed McCaleb, one of the early developers of the XRP Ledger. The original Bitcoin code even included a comment left by the mysterious creator of Bitcoin.

Afterward, Schwartz shared the reason why XRP Ledger developers opted to use the cryptographic options from Bitcoin instead of creating fresh ones.

"We did things that way in the very early days because we didn't want to be potentially facing criticism that our choices for those core crypto functions were less secure than Bitcoin's," mentioned Schwartz.

In other words, XRP Ledger developers opted to use Bitcoin's cryptographic options to avoid possible controversial security-related decisions when creating a fresh cryptocurrency network.

Later on, Vet asked Schwartz if their decision helped gain acceptance among Bitcoin supporters who looked at their protocol in its early stages.

Schwartz stated it was hard to say whether it helped or not.

Industry observers note that "It's hard to say. Obviously we never got those criticisms. But it's hard to know if we would have," Schwartz noted.

Additionally, the Ripple executive pointed out that it was uncertain whether the developers could have come up with better options if they had chosen to make their own cryptographic decisions.

"I'm not sure we would have come up with better ones had we made our own decisions anyway," Schwartz wrote.

It is worth noting that the original Bitcoin code copied in the early stages of the XRP Ledger is no longer present in the network's codebase.

According to Vet, the remaining parts of Satoshi Nakamoto's timekeeping code were deleted in December 2014 by former Ripple engineering lead Nik Bougalis.

There are two crucial cryptographic design decisions from Bitcoin that are still used on the XRP Ledger.
