  • Sources indicate that A Bitcoin address that had not moved coins since February 2011 transferred 75 BTC on Nov.
  • The address is listed as a defendant in a $250 billion lawsuit in Upcoming York Supreme Court, in which the plaintiffs are trying to have early Bitcoin wallets declared "lost." Galaxy Research said that several other addresses from the same list have also moved coins in 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Sources indicate that A Bitcoin address that had not moved coins since February 2011 transferred 75 BTC on Nov. 17, according to Galaxy Research. At the current price of $64,935 per BTC, the coins are worth around $4.87 million.

The address is listed as a defendant in a $250 billion lawsuit in Upcoming York Supreme Court, in which the plaintiffs are trying to have early Bitcoin wallets declared "lost." Galaxy Research said that several other addresses from the same list have also moved coins in 2026.

According to Galaxy Research analysts, early on Nov. 17, in block 976,209, the address 1ALpEWtXApR19hLXvcG8NfkPyGsUMhFPMS sent coins for the first time. It was first funded on Feb. 8, 2011. At that time, Bitcoin was trading at about $0.90. After 15.8 years, the coins went to an unknown address with a 399-satoshi fee, or about 26 cents, for a paper gain of more than 7,000,000%.

Sources indicate that onchain databases list the wallet as Noah Doe #3409 (Salomon Client Dusted). That label is how it ended up among the defendants in the high-profile case ABC Firm, XYZ Company, and Noah Doe v. John Does 1–39,069.

According to the lawsuit, an anonymous plaintiff using the pseudonym Noah Doe and two companies want the rights to 39,069 Bitcoin wallets that have not moved coins for more than five years. The plaintiffs noted that these wallets hold about 3.8 million BTC, and at the current price, the coins are worth around $250 billion.

The plaintiffs filed the lawsuit under New York's lost-and-found law, Article 7-B of the Personal Property Law. Under the law, a person who finds lost property has to give it to the police, and the property goes to the finder if the owner does not claim it in time. In the lawsuit, the plaintiffs valued each address at less than $10, and they argued that the waiting period for such items was one year.

They "found" dormant addresses with an algorithm, saved them onto USB flash drives and took them to the Newly introduced York Police Department (NYPD). Then they served the owners on the blockchain, through microtransactions with embedded messages (OP_RETURN). The practice is known as "dusting," and the campaign is tied to Salomon Brothers Strategic Advisors. Once the waiting period ran out, the plaintiffs asked the court to recognize the coins as theirs.

The case has been put on hold several times over motions to dismiss and amicus curiae briefs from outside experts. At a hearing on Sept. 8, the Bitcoin Policy Institute asked to intervene as a defendant, and The Digital Chamber asked to join the case as amicus curiae. Galaxy Research described it as a case "in which anonymous plaintiffs are seeking to claim legal title over Satoshi's coins.".

Galaxy Research's Will Owens, who attended the hearing, said that The Digital Chamber's arguments were "well pleaded" and that "the judge sounded sympathetic to them.".

It has been revealed that critics of the lawsuit argue that Article 7-B was written for things you can pick up and hand over for safekeeping. It wasn't written for blockchain records when the "finder" doesn't hold the private keys.

In September, Galaxy head of research Alex Thorn also remarked that the Lost and Found Property Law includes "protection from 'Noah Doe-style' dormancy attacks on legal ownership.".

How to Harness the Power of Human Interaction to Win Customers Over This Holiday Season

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Recent findings suggest that as the fourth quarter rolls around, entrepreneurs everywhere hope to close out a productive year.
  • AI can accomplish a lot, but it still falls short when it comes to the magic of personal touch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Recent findings suggest that as the fourth quarter rolls around, entrepreneurs everywhere hope to close out a productive year. This season sparks a flurry of activity for businesses, especially those eager to capitalize on fall and holiday shoppers. No matter your industry, the holiday season is the ideal moment to highlight the power of genuine human connection.

AI can accomplish a lot, but it still falls short when it comes to the magic of personal touch. It’s easy to see how positive human interaction can boost your business during the holidays, but these same tactics belong in your everyday playbook. Let’s explore a few simple ways the human touch can spark joy that goes far beyond your bottom line.

In a recent development, I have to confess, there are moments when I catch myself sounding like someone from an older generation. Every day, I remind my staff to return client calls promptly and reply to emails without delay. Though I’m only in my late 40s, I notice a shift in my younger colleagues. Like a fading sense of urgency and a dwindling desire for personal interaction.

Sources indicate that perhaps it’s a wish to sidestep conflict or uncomfortable conversations. I understand that urge. Still, I’ve learned that the fastest way to resolve a tough client situation is through genuine human touch. I’m not referring to physical touch, but honest, direct communication delivered with empathy and understanding. On the other hand, leading with human touch from the start can forge deeper bonds and lasting appreciation with customers.

In a recent development, you’ve probably heard the saying, “size matters.” While that might hold true in some cases, my own transcription company is small compared to many others. Yet, the personal touch we practice and that I encourage my team to deliver works just as well for medium and large businesses alike.

Most of our first interactions with clients begin on our website, where a potential customer fills out our contact form. That’s our first chance to connect personally, to reach out and add a human touch. Here’s an example of how a team member might respond to a website inquiry.

According to recent reports, “Thanks for reaching out, Jane. We’d love to assist you with your court hearing transcripts. When do you need them completed and sent back?”.

Sources indicate that let’s unpack our initial email. First, we always address the person by name. If they include a title, we use it, whether it’s Dr. Smith or Detective Jones. Second, we acknowledge their inquiry as promptly as possible, ideally within 15 minutes. Finally, we ask for permission to connect more personally. A phone conversation with a potential customer lets us highlight our services and, even more importantly, our commitment to detail.

Industry observers note that most people appreciate the chance to talk by phone. For those who prefer email, there are still plenty of ways to add a personal touch throughout the exchange. Whether we’re on the phone or typing an email, we make it a point to ask open-ended questions that encourage the other person to share more. This is a classic strategy sales trainers recommend everywhere.

Sources indicate that the holiday season offers your team even more chances to make a lasting impression through personal interaction. We keep it simple with a cheerful “Happy Holidays,” but if a client mentions a specific celebration, i.e., Thanksgiving, Christmas, Hanukkah or Kwanzaa, then we ask how they are enjoying their favorite season.

Finally, our team always aims to have the last word. When a customer pays an invoice, we don’t just send an automated “Thank you for your payment.” Instead, we follow up with a personal email to our main contact, giving us one more opportunity to add a genuine human touch.

Sources indicate that what exactly will your business or company gain through human touch? Trust. Customers, more specifically, individuals, want to know they can trust you to deliver a service or product.

It’s true that most companies can build some trust without much human interaction. If you add a personal touch, it speeds up the process and makes it feel more genuine. Too often, human interaction only happens when something goes wrong. While it’s smart to use a personal approach to solve problems, starting every client relationship with a human touch lays a strong foundation for when challenges pop up later.

People with a personal relationship with an employee or organization respond to challenges very differently than those without one. That’s simply human nature.

According to recent reports, personally, I get frustrated when I can’t reach a real person with a question or concern. Endless phone trees and chatbots that never connect you to a human leave me feeling anything but trust. Here are a few ways to boost human interaction:.

Sources indicate that if Emily Post, the famed etiquette expert of the early 20th century, were still with us, I’m sure she’d have plenty to say about the power of handwritten notes. Even though I haven’t found a definitive study on their impact, my own experience tells me that few things leave a stronger impression than a personally written letter or note.

I think the magic of a handwritten note starts with the effort it takes. Printing a form letter or invoice is easy, but writing a note by hand and addressing the envelope takes real time and care. Even jotting a quick sentence or two at the bottom of a printed letter can make a lasting impression.

Industry observers note that last month, I received a statement from the firm that acquired the self-storage facility I use. Because of a glitch when switching back-end systems, I didn’t receive an invoice for a couple of months, which resulted in the fresh owner placing their lock on my unit. A quick phone call resolved the situation and also gave the new company a chance to introduce themselves.

The next week, I received an invoice with a handwritten note from the owner. He apologized for the mistake, thanked me for my business and invited me to reach out directly with any questions or concerns. Even with a rate increase, his personal effort left a positive impression.

It has been revealed that the holiday season in the fourth quarter gives businesses a golden chance to thank both new and loyal customers for their support. Gift baskets, charitable donations in their name, party invites or even a simple greeting card (ideally signed by a real person) are all thoughtful ways to share holiday cheer.

But why limit these gestures to just the holidays? Why not carry these strategies through all 12 months of the year?

Many entrepreneurs and business owners use the holidays as a chance for personal, even face-to-face, connections. Each holiday season, I spend a few weeks personally delivering homemade gourmet treats to clients across Colorado. Without an outside sales team, these personal holiday visits have become a winning strategy for us. Plus, they love and eagerly anticipate the gourmet homemade goodies I deliver.

According to recent reports, this also reminds me that personal visits shouldn’t happen only once a year. In fact, they should be a regular occurrence. Personal interaction, especially when it comes from the owner, is a powerful strategy that deserves a permanent spot on the calendar.

According to recent reports, don’t forget to reach out to customers you haven’t connected with in a while. The holidays are a perfect time to show your appreciation, but make it a goal to check in with every customer at least once a quarter.

Here’s a reminder not to neglect your internal staff: Employees and team members need and deserve recognition. Schedule a lunch, dinner or get-together to show appreciation and thank everyone for making your clients and customers feel valued.

As the fourth quarter rolls around, entrepreneurs everywhere hope to close out a productive year. This season sparks a flurry of activity for businesses, especially those eager to capitalize on fall and holiday shoppers. No matter your industry, the holiday season is the ideal moment to highlight the power of genuine human connection.

It has been revealed that AI can accomplish a lot, but it still falls short when it comes to the magic of personal touch. It’s easy to see how positive human interaction can boost your business during the holidays, but these same tactics belong in your everyday playbook. Let’s explore a few simple ways the human touch can spark joy that goes far beyond your bottom line.

I have to confess, there are moments when I catch myself sounding like someone from an older generation. Every day, I remind my staff to return client calls promptly and reply to emails without delay. Though I’m only in my late 40s, I notice a shift in my younger colleagues. Like a fading sense of urgency and a dwindling desire for personal interaction.

Sources indicate that sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, declared a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the manufacturer plans to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

According to recent reports, sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, noted Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

It has been revealed that “This is a really important blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he said. “We have to take new technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”.

Industry observers note that while the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky said. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

According to recent reports, berdichevsky stated Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

In August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The company must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

The startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

The company has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round announced in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

In a recent development, seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

According to recent reports, group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently confirmed prepares for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky stated.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our organization’s history,” he remarked.

The first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

In a recent development, “None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky noted. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”.

Nanbeige4.3-33B Ties Qwen3.8-27B on Intelligence Index, but Spends 44% More Output Tokens

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1082 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nanbeige4.3-33B matches Qwen3.8-27B at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index but uses 158K output tokens per task against 110K.
  • In a recent development, two models just posted the same score.
  • In a recent development, nanbeige4.3-33B, a dense 33-billion-parameter reasoning model from the foundation model team at BOSS Zhipin, scores 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Nanbeige4.3-33B matches Qwen3.8-27B at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index but uses 158K output tokens per task against 110K. Here is what that costs locally.

In a recent development, two models just posted the same score. One needed 158,000 output tokens per task to get there. The other needed 110,000.

In a recent development, nanbeige4.3-33B, a dense 33-billion-parameter reasoning model from the foundation model team at BOSS Zhipin, scores 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5. According to Artificial Analysis's evaluation, published November 5, that matches Qwen3.8 27B at its xhigh reasoning setting. The model is open weights under Apache 2.0, accepts text only, and has a 524K-token context window.

Behind the tie sits a gap in effort. Artificial Analysis claims Nanbeige used 158K output tokens per Intelligence Index task against 110K for Qwen3.8 27B, about 44% more. That weighted average covers answer and reasoning tokens across all nine v5 evaluations, including agentic tool-use turns. For anyone running these models, tokens translate into time, electricity or money, so the same score doesn't mean the same cost.

It has been revealed that the Intelligence Index v5 combines nine evaluations, among them AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, Terminal-Bench 4.0, FrontierCode 2.0 and AA-Omniscience. A score of 20 puts Nanbeige well above the 6 of Muse Glimmer, a 30B model in the same comparison. Artificial Analysis also notes that Nanbeige sets a new Pareto-optimal point for Intelligence Index against total parameters, since both it and Qwen3.8 27B are dense models. A larger mixture-of-experts model like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, by contrast, scores 33 while activating only 16B parameters per token.

It has been revealed that the model card Nanbeige's lab published on Hugging Face describes the base model, positioned as the flagship teacher for the Nanbeige4.3 series. The lab claims it will distill agentic capabilities into smaller models, such as an upcoming 3B version. On base-model benchmarks, the card reveals 66.9 on MMLU-Pro against 59.3 for Gemma4-31B-Base. Those figures belong to the base model and are separate from the reasoning model's Intelligence Index result.

The two models reach 20 by different routes. Nanbeige scores 30% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 against 6% for Qwen, and 16% on the CritPt v2 Hard Subset against 4%. It also edges Qwen on AutomationBench-AA, 53% to 48%.

In a recent development, elsewhere, it falls behind. On AA-Briefcase v1.1 it scores 1162 Elo against 1391, on FrontierCode 2.0 11% against 15%, and on HLE-Diamond 7% against 15%. The knowledge test tells the most distinctive story. On AA-Omniscience v1.1, Nanbeige scores -4 against Qwen's -6, with an 18% hallucination rate against 29%. Yet it answers only 29% of questions against 43%, declines 71% of them and gets 12% correct against 17%.

For general question answering, Qwen's higher accuracy is the better result.

Output tokens aren't a vanity metric. A reasoning model writes out its thinking as tokens, and every one costs decode time. If both models ran at the same speed on the same hardware, Nanbeige would take about 44% longer to finish a typical task.

Local decoding adds a second factor. Generation is usually limited by memory bandwidth, because each new token requires reading the model's weights, and a 33B dense model reads about 20% more weight data per token than a 27B dense model. Assuming the same quantization and the same memory-bound hardware, those two effects compound to roughly 1.7 times the wall-clock time per task. That figure is a back-of-the-envelope calculation, not a measured result.

It has been revealed that nor is there a hosted alternative to soften the blow. Artificial Analysis lists no confirmed public first-party or third-party APIs for Nanbeige, so unlike Qwen, which is sold per token through Alibaba's API, the cost is the hardware you run it on and the time it takes.

Artificial Analysis describes the model as small enough to run locally on a laptop, which holds true with a caveat. The weights are published in BF16, which at 33 billion parameters means roughly 66 GB, far beyond almost any laptop. At 8-bit, the weights fall to about 33 GB, and at 4-bit to about 17 GB, plus memory for the context cache. A machine with 24 GB of unified memory or more can plausibly hold a 4-bit build, though a long context will push it.

In a recent development, the vendor's own quickstart points the other way. The card's SGLang and vLLM examples both set tensor parallelism across four GPUs, which suggests the reference deployment is a multi-GPU server. Its Transformers example also enables trust_remote_code=True, which runs code from the repository. Reading that code first is the safer move, as is serving the model through vLLM or SGLang instead.

Industry observers note that quantization changes the model, too. The Intelligence Index numbers come from Artificial Analysis's own runs, so a 4-bit local build may score somewhat lower, or generate different token counts, than the version they evaluated.

This release is a clean example of why a headline score isn't enough. Nanbeige delivers Qwen-level results at 33B, with strengths in terminal tasks and physics reasoning and a more cautious answering style. The price for those strengths is length.

Sources indicate that anyone choosing between the two should run both on their own workload and record three numbers: the score on their tasks, output tokens per task and seconds per task on their hardware. For terminal-heavy, agentic work, Nanbeige's profile may justify the longer runs. For knowledge-heavy or latency-sensitive work, Qwen's shorter, more accurate answers look stronger.

Three signals are worth watching next: whether the 3B distilled version keeps the model's strengths, whether other labs report the same token behavior, and whether anyone publishes quantized local benchmarks. Until then, the simplest summary is also the most accurate: same score, different bill.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ripple-backed XRP treasury tech giant Evernorth Holdings has disclosed a significant decrease in the book value of its crypto asset holdings, with total impairment charges amounting to around $505 million before going public on Nasdaq.

Per an SEC filing on Nov. 13, the 346.3 million XRP tokens that Evernorth Holdings owned had a book value of just $341.9 million as of Sept. 30, 2026.

This is compared to the firm's initial accounting of the crypto assets at roughly $846.6 million, with an average acquisition or contribution price of $2.44 per XRP. This represents a nearly 60% decline in book value.

As per the latest filing, Evernorth recorded around $271 million in XRP impairment charges in the first nine months of 2026. This is in addition to the $233.7 million in impairment charges recorded in 2025.

Interestingly, only $6.9 million of the recent impairment charges occurred in the third quarter.

This also explains why Evernorth's XRP assets had a book value so far below their market value at the end of September.

In a recent development, evernorth calculates impairments based on the lowest observable intraday price of XRP for each batch of tokens acquired. Once the assets are written down, the firm is unable to reverse the previous losses if the price rises.

According to recent reports, for reference, on Sept. 30, XRP closed the day trading at around $1.49 on Coinbase. At that price, Evernorth's 346.3 million XRP tokens would have been worth roughly $516 million, much higher than the disclosed book value of $341.9 million.

The recent disclosure comes around a month after Evernorth completed its business combination with Armada Acquisition Corp. II on Oct. 9. It started trading on Nasdaq under the symbol XRPN on Oct. 12.

Following the business combination, Evernorth held around 473 million XRP tokens and had also raised gross cash proceeds of around $300 million.

Its investors include Ripple, SBI Group, Arrington Capital, Pantera Capital, Kraken and GSR.

According to recent reports, on Oct. 14, Evernorth announced collaborations with Ripple, Kraken, Coinbase and BitGo to implement institutional investment strategies starting in Q4 2026.

Meanwhile, its latest SEC filing did not include details on the amount of XRP deployed to generate yield or the returns generated from it.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta employees have raised concerns about the organization’s Muse AI agent after receiving unprompted notifications that tapped into private information, according to internal posts seen by Reuters.

In one example, a Meta staffer reported that Muse sent her a reminder on her personal phone to respond to a message from her sister on the encrypted messaging service Signal.

“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee posted.

A Meta colleague also shared that he got unsolicited chats related to apps he had not connected and discovered Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on Android phones, Reuters reported.

Another employee posted that during his chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, Muse said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”.

Other random Muse messages also took Meta workers aback, including a question about parental control over access to their child’s data and a conversation about picking up a coffee table that raised concern over “possible cross-account context leak.”.

In response to the internal posts about Muse, a member of Meta’s Superintelligence team stated the agent appeared to be hallucinating due to built-in prompts that were designed to engage users between sessions, according to Reuters.

“These (hallucinations) unfortunately bias towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks,” he stated, adding that other cases involved “crypto-related things too, like giving people updates on their Bitcoin balances.”.

The random, out-of-context messages were confirmed as hallucinations.

A Meta spokesperson said employee testing is core to product development and is meant to generate feedback in order to implement privacy safeguards, adding that employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public does and that some functions aren’t available elsewhere.

As for the Muse messages that referred to encrypted Signal chats, the spokesperson pointed out that Android consumers have the option to grant apps notification access, which they must opt in to and is not specific to Muse.

“With Mac, to allow Muse to work on your behalf, you not only need to click allow for accessibility and screen recording, but after that it takes you to a settings screen where you once again need to confirm and turn this on,” Meta explained.

Recent findings suggest that since Muse was debuted in September, it’s been downloaded more than 10 million times, becoming one of the fastest-growing apps ever. It’s also key to the social-media giant’s plan to generate billions of dollars in revenue from AI.

But other companies are blocking Muse and other AI agents. For example, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon noted the bank won’t allow agents to access customer accounts and act on their behalf.

Similarly, Amazon won’t let Muse shop on its e-commerce platform and is already fighting to keep out Perplexity’s AI agents.

The process of raising those barriers, however, also entails network upgrades that may be contributing to a sudden surge in outages.

In a recent development, in recent weeks, companies like Chase, Wells Fargo, United Airlines, Apple, and Microsoft saw temporary service disruptions. U.S. officials have mentioned there’s no evidence of cyberattacks, suggesting software patches were deployed before all the bugs were worked out.

In a recent development, because AI tools can find vulnerabilities faster than companies can safely fix them, the pressure to fix them right away is straining systems that were never designed for that speed, Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, told the Financial Times.

In an interview with Fortune’s Catherina Gioino, Mark Giles, director of Downdetector parent company Ookla Research, stated there’s nothing linking the outages.

“This is a substantial blip, but it’s kind of on par for the course for what we’re seeing in terms of those longer-term trends,” he remarked. “Most of the time they’re fairly self-contained and remedied quite promptly. It’s the ones where you can’t withdraw money or you can’t access your emails that really get the headlines.”.

Sources indicate that at age 23, Phil Shawe was pursuing an MBA at NYU when he had a business idea that made some people around him skeptical. Why spend money on business school, thousands of dollars, only to start a small translation company?

It has been revealed that shawe saw an opening. Advertising agencies, law firms and big corporations needed language services. He believed he could deliver something better than what was currently on the market.

“I met my former partner in business school, and she had worked at the largest translation firm at the time, Berlitz,” Shawe claims in a new interview with Entrepreneur. “She worked there in New York, and they were constantly unable to satisfy clients. We theorized that there was a better mousetrap to build in the language business.”.

According to recent reports, in 1992, Shawe and his business partner, Liz Elting, co-founded TransPerfect from his NYU dorm room. They didn’t have a large financial backer underwriting their ambitions. They financed the business themselves, leaned on credit cards and tried to find customers.

First, the founders had to persuade someone to hire them.

“We would basically cold-call till our fingers bled,” Shawe says.

Sources indicate that they also faxed prospects and sent mailers containing information and brochures. As projects came in, they built a network of linguists to handle the work. Shawe’s description of the early sales strategy is simple: “Brute force clients in the door.”.

In a recent development, shawe has since helped turn that operation into a business generating $1.32 billion in annual revenue. He notes that TransPerfect now has more than 10,000 employees, whose work extends from translating contracts and supporting global drug studies to developing software and helping companies implement AI.

It has been revealed that shawe states that about half of the organization’s revenue still comes from language translation services. The rest comes from technology consulting and other businesses shaped around customer needs.

According to recent reports, as TransPerfect has grown, so has Shawe’s net worth. According to the Forbes billionaires list, Shawe, 57, is at the moment worth $1.7 billion.

It has been revealed that transPerfect produced about $400,000 in revenue in its first year, Shawe indicates. He recalls that the manufacturer broke even that year, with little choice but to keep spending below what it brought in.

Industry observers note that the founders reinvested in the company as it grew. There was an exception to the largely self-financed approach: In 1998, Shawe claims, they separated the technology business from the traditional translation operation and raised $4.1 million, with Deutsche Bank as the lead investor.

Industry observers note that after the internet bubble burst, he and his partner used their own money to return investors’ original capital. Shawe later bought out his partner in 2018.

It has been revealed that shawe does not credit the company’s rise entirely to persistence. TransPerfect arrived as the internet and globalization created new connections across borders. The founders worked hard, but the timing helped.

However, as the company expanded, landing work was not the toughest problem. Shawe indicates hiring and retaining people who could deliver the work became harder. The founders could not oversee every project or client relationship, so training employees became increasingly important.

Growth also taught Shawe a costly lesson about the difference between a customer’s promise and a binding commitment.

Early on, a client indicated that a substantial amount of business was coming. TransPerfect opened an Atlanta office, placed people on-site and made significant investments to prepare. Then the customer changed course, leaving the company financially exposed.

“It almost put us out of business,” Shawe says.

According to recent reports, he says that situation was his most expensive mistake as a founder. The error was investing heavily in a venture without adequate contractual protection. His takeaway was not to make massive capital commitments for business that a customer has only verbally agreed to provide.

According to recent reports, transPerfect started with cold outreach. Keeping customers helped it scale. “If you want a business to grow, the most vital thing you can do is retain your customers,” Shawe claims.

For TransPerfect, that meant hitting deadlines and delivering projects in the formats clients expect. Consistently performing well could turn a customer contact into an internal advocate, or someone willing to recommend the company to another team or division.

Recent findings suggest that shawe says referrals between divisions of large corporations is an important source of business. TransPerfect prefers to obtain fresh customers through recommendations from within an organization, and much of its sales activity now involves expanding services for existing customers.

Industry observers note that transPerfect also organized around industries. Once it had enough banking work, for example, it could build a dedicated finance division staffed with people who understood that sector. It applied the same approach to law firms, life sciences and luxury brands.

The company’s goal is to become a trusted advisor, not simply a supplier accepting translation orders. Listening to customers opened doors. For example, legal translation clients needed help with electronic discovery, or finding and processing digital information for litigation. TransPerfect expanded into those services, and Shawe states the e-discovery and litigation-support business is on pace to generate $160 million or more this year.

“E-discovery and litigation support is not something that we started in the dorm room, but over the years enough of our customers communicated to us that they needed better or different services in this field, and that’s what drew us into it,” Shawe indicates.

He added that the business is now a “huge contributor” to the firm’s annual revenue.

Industry observers note that transPerfect faces newly introduced advancements like AI and rapid translation features from tech giants like Apple and Google. Shawe states that TransPerfect must bring new technology to customers.

“We want to be the ones constantly disrupting our own business,” he says.

In a recent development, shawe has witnessed several waves of technology reshape translation, including neural machine translation, or AI that automatically translates text with advanced technology, and now large language models, or AI programs trained on massive amounts of text data. Shawe says each change has created ways to accomplish more with fewer resources.

He notes that if formatting a multilingual manual once required 40 hours, and software can reduce that work to an hour or 15 minutes, TransPerfect should introduce the software, even if it loses billable hours.

“It might decrease our revenue in the short term, but it’s going to cement our client relationship and allow us to grow the business with that customer in the long term,” Shawe says.

Sources indicate that transPerfect can go beyond translating words and help businesses use language technology effectively. Shawe says customers continue to turn to the tech giant for additional languages and higher-risk content even as automation handles more work.

He advises young founders to “raise as little money as possible” and “show real revenues as much as you can.”.

If he were starting from scratch with limited money and no network, he says he would focus on building relationships with customers and team members.

“These contacts that you make when you’re young, they compound like interest, and the value of those relationships also compounds,” Shawe says.

It has been revealed that at age 23, Phil Shawe was pursuing an MBA at NYU when he had a business idea that made some people around him skeptical. Why spend money on business school, thousands of dollars, only to start a small translation firm?

Shawe saw an opening. Advertising agencies, law firms and big corporations needed language services. He believed he could deliver something better than what was presently on the market.

Industry observers note that “I met my former partner in business school, and she had worked at the largest translation manufacturer at the time, Berlitz,” Shawe claims in a new interview with Entrepreneur. “She worked there in New York, and they were constantly unable to satisfy clients. We theorized that there was a better mousetrap to build in the language business.”.

‘Absurd ambition’: Pulumi expands into software delivery with AI agents that ship and fix code

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too big to take on.
  • The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting latest software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too big to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting latest software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

Recent findings suggest that “The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” said Joe Duffy, the company’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how big we’re willing to dream.”.

Recent findings suggest that the ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The manufacturer has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy stated there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The firm isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

In a recent development, pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the company in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The new products take that approach further:.

To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Duffy mentioned he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” remarked Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”.

Both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise plans.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy remarked.

Recent findings suggest that AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy said. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Sources indicate that duffy said many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The newly introduced products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

In a recent development, plenty of company: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He remarked Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The new products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he said.

“This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy noted. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”.

Bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy remarked.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy said no launch in the tech giant’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

It has been revealed that the business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy noted. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Duffy stated Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the organization, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy said, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

Sources indicate that about 40 of the company’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy said Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building upcoming products.

According to recent reports, despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the organization, Duffy remarked Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”.

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy mentioned Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”.

Bank of America has disclosed a position in an XRP exchange-traded fund in its latest quarterly 13F filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing, dated Nov. 16, reveals that the bank held 13,260 shares of the futures-based Volatility Shares XRP ETF (XRPI), worth about $106,600, at the end of the third quarter.

Sources indicate that bank of America held 13,000 shares of the fund in the first quarter and 13,260 shares in the second quarter, according to its earlier 13F filings. The same filing lists more than $685 million in BlackRock's IBIT, $13.58 million in Bitwise and $950,000 in VanEck.

In a recent development, seven major banks disclosed XRP fund holdings worth a total of $29.4 million in filings published between Nov. 9 and Nov. 16. Italy's Intesa Sanpaolo disclosed the largest stake among them, at $27.21 million. The bank held 712,319 shares of the Grayscale XRP Trust ETF, worth about $20.52 million, and it also opened a newly introduced position of 402,750 shares in the Bitwise XRP ETF, worth about $6.7 million.

UBS and Morgan Stanley disclosed XRP fund holdings of $1.91 million and $116,000, respectively. Most of the UBS position was in the Volatility Shares XRP ETF, and Morgan Stanley held funds from Franklin, REX-Osprey and Bitwise.

JPMorgan Chase held 539 shares of the Bitwise fund, worth about $9,000, and National Bank of Canada held 330 shares of the same fund, worth about $5,500. Bank of Montreal held REX-Osprey and ProShares Ultra XRP shares worth $4,300.

The crypto portfolio of Goldman Sachs grew to $2.64 billion by the end of September, according to its 13F filing. The bank held about $1.28 billion in Bitcoin ETFs, and BlackRock's IBIT and Fidelity's FBTC accounted for $778 million and $398 million of that amount, respectively. Goldman also held about $1.22 billion in Ether funds, and BlackRock's ETHA accounted for $603 million of that amount.

It has been revealed that goldman held $144 million in XRP ETFs at the end of the third quarter, up from $87 million at the end of the second quarter. The bank's 13F filing for the first quarter showed no XRP or Solana ETF holdings, and Goldman still held no Solana funds at the end of September.

The bank held shares of five spot XRP funds from Franklin Templeton, Bitwise, Canary, Grayscale and 21Shares, and its Franklin Templeton position was worth almost $48 million.

Besides, trading firm Jane Street reported $23.5 million in XRP funds, and Simplex Trading disclosed a $14 million stake in the Grayscale fund. EP Wealth Advisors raised its Volatility Shares XRP ETF holding by 37% to 18,400 shares, worth about $148,000.

Industry observers note that A 13F filing only highlights long positions as of Sept. 30. It doesn't show whether the banks hedge those holdings with shorts, or what they did with the shares in October and November. Since then, XRP has fallen below $1, and on Tuesday morning, XRP was trading at $0.966.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Two officials at the Federal Emergency Management Agency told the Washington Post they were concerned about the outages and were having trouble believing they were a coincidence.
  • One official took out extra cash, and the other reported being bombarded with questions from former classmates asking whether they should prepare for an emergency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Trump administration has insisted that the recent surge in network outages isn’t due to a cyberattack, but those responsible for the federal government’s emergency response aren’t so sure.

Two officials at the Federal Emergency Management Agency told the Washington Post they were concerned about the outages and were having trouble believing they were a coincidence.

One official took out extra cash, and the other reported being bombarded with questions from former classmates asking whether they should prepare for an emergency.

It has been revealed that “There is nothing on this scale that has happened before in this many sectors this close together,” one of the officials told the Post. “This is scary, and there is no leadership.”.

FEMA didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Sources indicate that even before everything appeared to break down, Americans were already on edge after the Pentagon rolled out an initiative called FORTRESS, which seeks to ensure that every major U.S. military base can run for 90 days without outside help if a war cuts off power and supply chains.

Then came a month of cyberattacks that hit hundreds of companies and institutions around the world. The hacking spree was so widespread that it was dubbed “Black October.” The Nvidia spy scandal also didn’t help sentiment.

Industry observers note that last Thursday, Microsoft’s email and other office tools went down. Last Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all planes for more than four hours. It later blamed a copper wire that was being upgraded to a fiber-optic cable.

Days later, companies like Chase, Wells Fargo, United Airlines, and Apple saw temporary service disruptions. The National Security Agency’s internal classified communications network also suffered an outage, further fraying nerves.

U.S. officials have mentioned there’s no evidence of cyberattacks, suggesting network upgrades meant to patch newly uncovered vulnerabilities were deployed hastily before all the bugs were worked out.

Industry observers note that director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday that “these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.”.

Recent findings suggest that despite the administration’s denials that cybersecurity was an problem, the White House removed U.S. National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross on Thursday. CNN also reported Friday that mentioned the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its nationwide criminal information database—the second such breach in recent months.

Recent findings suggest that the steady drumbeat of alarming news has pushed many Americans into panic mode. Costco and Walmart have seen more shoppers stocking up on emergency supplies.

In a recent development, “Consumer anxiety, following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media, have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at Costco,” Mizuho analyst David Bellinger wrote in a recent note.

Adding to the unease was the U.K. government’s campaign urging Britons to keep canned food, bottled water, and cash on hand to get through three days of disruption.

And for good measure, the stock market has been pummeled with some of the worst declines since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic as investors fear the end of the AI boom could take the U.S. economy down with it.

Recent findings suggest that the cumulative effect of all the disruptions has caused Americans to fear the worst. Chuck Amasio, a 68-year-old from Rahway, Newly introduced Jersey, who was stuck at Newark Liberty International Airport, told the Associated Press last week “there’s a lot of weird stuff going on” and wondered if it was all part of some form of attack.

Sources indicate that “We talk about how wars aren’t done with bombs anymore,” he added. “They shut down airspace or a power grid. They can cripple an economy.”.

But in an interview with Fortune’s Catherina Gioino, Mark Giles, director of Downdetector parent organization Ookla Research, said there’s nothing linking the outages.

“This is a significant blip, but it’s kind of on par for the course for what we’re seeing in terms of those longer-term trends,” he explained. “Most of the time they’re fairly self-contained and remedied quite promptly. It’s the ones where you can’t withdraw money or you can’t access your emails that really get the headlines.”.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1710 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Entrepreneur ↗ Open Full Page

Want to Write Your First Novel? Here Are 10 Books to Read Before Picking Up Your Pen.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1710 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You have an idea for a fiction novel that you can’t stop thinking about.
  • So you open a blank document, type a sentence, pause for a moment, then delete it.
  • Industry observers note that before you try to answer every question on your own, turn to your bookshelf.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You have an idea for a fiction novel that you can’t stop thinking about. Maybe it’s a character, a setting or a scene you’ve played out in your head countless times. No matter what it is, you want to explore this newly introduced world.

So you open a blank document, type a sentence, pause for a moment, then delete it. Faced with an empty page, you wonder how your seed of an idea is supposed to become an entire book. How can a formless thought take shape?

Industry observers note that before you try to answer every question on your own, turn to your bookshelf. Learn the craft of writing from people who have done it before you. How does a writer make you care about a stranger, a made-up character, within the first few lines? What keeps you reading when little seems to happen?

Then there’s the ending. How does an ending feel both surprising and inevitable?

In a recent development, the following 10 books offer a place to explore those questions. Some explain how to build a plot or develop a character. Others help you manage doubt and pay attention. They all treat fiction as a craft you can study. They can also keep you manufacturer as you begin writing a story of your own and remind you that you are not alone in your pursuit of writing a novel.

On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft.

It has been revealed that author Stephen King has published over 60 novels and sold more than 350 million copies of his books globally. In this book, he combines his personal story of becoming a writer with a practical account of how he works. In the autobiographical sections, he reveals his early encounters with storytelling, his struggles before getting published for the first time and how writing fits into the rest of his life. He also explores the practical aspects of writing, including vocabulary, grammar, description, dialogue and revision. His approach is direct and conversational. The book also features a marked-up manuscript that reveals actual revisions, which can be helpful for writers thinking about the process of editing. Overall, King offers encouragement and technical advice for first-time novelists.

Bird by Bird: Some Instructions on Writing and Life.

Anne Lamott starts this book with a family story. Her brother left a report about birds until the last minute and felt overwhelmed by everything he had to do. Their father told him to take it bird by bird, inspiring the title of the book. That small instruction becomes the book’s central approach to writing. Instead of confronting the project as an impossible whole, attend to one manageable piece at a time. Lamott applies that approach to rough drafts and the emotional confusion of creative work. She offers humor and permission to produce messy drafts. Her advice is to reduce the task into bite-sized parts, accept imperfection and continue even when there is no guarantee of a future reward.

Writing Down the Bones: Freeing the Writer Within.

In this book, popular author Natalie Goldberg approaches writing as a practice strengthened through repetition. She offers short reflections and exercises that help writers get words onto the page before their inner judgment shuts them down. The exercises provide a low-pressure space for discovering memories, images and even unexpected connections. The focus is on developing an open relationship with the act of writing. Goldberg pushes writers to keep the hand moving and resist the urge to cross out thoughts immediately. These small habits help the writer notice more and censor less when creating material. If you spend more time evaluating possible sentences rather than writing them, this is the book for you. It has sold more than one million copies.

Story Genius: How to Use Brain Science to Go Beyond Outlining and Write a Riveting Novel (Before You Waste Three Years Writing 327 Pages That Go Nowhere).

Author Lisa Cron is a story coach, speaker and author who has previously worked as a literary agent. She asks writers to look beneath the surface events of a story. In other words, an unusual situation or dramatic accident is not enough by itself. What matters is how that event affects a particular person, given that person’s unique worldview. Her method places the protagonist’s internal struggle at the center of the novel’s development. The book moves from an initial idea to a developed blueprint, including scenes. Its aim is to connect incidents through a protagonist’s changing interiority. Read this when you know what happens in your novel but cannot explain why it matters to the main character living through it.

According to recent reports, save the Cat! Writes a Novel: The Last Book On Novel Writing You’ll Ever Need.

Jessica Brody is the bestselling author of more than 20 novels, mainly young adult fiction. This book organizes story structure around 15 major developments, extending from the opening image to the finale. It also introduces 10 story categories based on patterns of conflict and transformation, giving writers ways to understand the kind of narrative they are building. The appeal is clarity. The writer can examine the purpose of different turning points in their novel. What introduces the central journey? When does the situation change? How does the ending express what the protagonist has learned? Read this if your first novel feels exciting in fragments but isn’t coming together as a whole.

Plot & Structure (Write Great Fiction).

Industry observers note that former trial lawyer James Scott Bell offers a practical guide to creating a plot and understanding how its parts fit together. He addresses the relationship between plot and structure and the differences between commercial and literary fiction. The emphasis is on usable techniques. Bell’s central framework is called LOCK, which stands for lead, objective, confrontation and knockout. These elements direct attention toward a compelling central character, a clear goal, meaningful opposition and a strong ending. Using these attributes, you can decide if a story has enough pressure and direction to sustain the reader’s interest. What is your protagonist trying to achieve? What prevents success? What would make the resolution satisfying?

Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story.

Author Ursula K. Le Guin turns her attention to the language by which a story reaches the reader. Her writing guide combines discussion with exercises. She walks readers through drills in storytelling, point of view and grammar. The exercises make this a book to use actively. Le Guin says that the work of a sentence is to carry the reader to the next one. She addresses how to handle exposition, or how to incorporate information into a story instead of allowing explanation to bring it to a halt. Her approach connects elements sometimes treated separately, like language and pacing. The value of this book is helping readers hear and inspect their prose. A promising plot still needs solid sentences that keep the story moving.

This style manual was privately printed in 1918 for Cornell University students by English professor William Strunk Jr., then published more widely by Harcourt in 1920. Strunk’s former student and author E. B. White revised and expanded the volume in 1959. This book concentrates on constructing clear prose. It is short, about 100 pages, which means it is perfect to consult regularly as you write. Its usefulness lies in directing a writer’s attention toward language. A novelist might be absorbed in a character’s choices while giving too little thought to how to clearly communicate those behaviors in a sentence. Strunk and White set the stage for authors to learn the conventions of clear prose. They provide a foundation from which to make deliberate stylistic choices that enhance a reader’s experience.

The Writing Life: The Classic Essay Collection on the Creative Process.

Annie Dillard, a Pulitzer Prize-winning novelist with experience writing fiction and nonfiction, published poetry, essays, prose and literary criticism. In The Writing Life, she offers a reflection on creative writing, not a step-by-step manual. She considers the difficulty and uncertainty of the writing process. A line of words can lead a writer into unfamiliar territory, but they may not know where to go next. What first appears promising might actually be a dead end, while a seemingly incidental encounter might become the real subject. Dillard preserves a place for the parts of writing that remain difficult, even when the writer is attentive and experienced. She offers perspective on the patience and seriousness of writing.

Refuse to Be Done: How to Write and Rewrite a Novel in Three Drafts.

In a recent development, writer and teacher Matt Bell treats revision as a central part of novel writing. His guide divides the process into three broad stages, giving each step a different purpose. The first move helps writers generate material and move through the initial draft. The second focuses on reworking the narrative through outlining, modeling and rewriting. The third step turns toward a layered polishing process. This final stage breaks revision into specific operations, deconstructing a large and potentially overwhelming task into a series of more manageable actions. This book is worth reading before writing the first page. It offers a practical guide to making a manuscript stronger.

Sources indicate that you have an idea for a fiction novel that you can’t stop thinking about. Maybe it’s a character, a setting or a scene you’ve played out in your head countless times. No matter what it is, you want to explore this new world.

Recent findings suggest that so you open a blank document, type a sentence, pause for a moment, then delete it. Faced with an empty page, you wonder how your seed of an idea is supposed to become an entire book. How can a formless thought take shape?

Before you try to answer every question on your own, turn to your bookshelf. Learn the craft of writing from people who have done it before you. How does a writer make you care about a stranger, a made-up character, within the first few lines? What keeps you reading when little seems to happen?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Galaxy Digital CEO Mike Novogratz noted that the odds of Bitcoin hitting $90,000 by the end of 2026 are slim in light of prevailing macroeconomic headwinds and the growing likelihood that the Federal Reserve may hike interest rates.

During a live event with Anthony Scaramucci at the Digital Assets Forum in New York City, Novogratz was asked if Bitcoin could get back to $90,000 by the end of this year.

"Less likely than it was. You need something to happen," Novogratz mentioned.

His gloomy outlook comes as Bitcoin has struggled to rebound after a devastating drop that saw its price dip as low as $62,000 over the weekend. Bitcoin's price stood at around $64,600 on Nov. 17. The largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization has declined for six consecutive weeks.

A shift in the U.S. monetary policy outlook, namely the prospect of more rate hikes from the Federal Reserve, has been largely to blame for Bitcoin's decline, according to Novogratz.

"At the start of the year, everybody thought the Fed was going to be cutting now," he stated.

But high inflation and ongoing supply shocks have forced investors to readjust their expectations.

Industry observers note that "Inflation's going up. We've got inflation going up," Novogratz noted, warning that inflationary pressures could become increasingly entrenched.

"The Fed's going to hike. At least two more, probably three more," he stated.

Novogratz predicted that the Fed would raise rates by 25 basis points in December and then hike again at its next meeting.

According to recent reports, he said that higher rates, at least in the near term, tend to weigh on Bitcoin. But the higher cost of government borrowing could eventually provide support for the cryptocurrency.

"Yeah, later," he mentioned in response to the suggestion that higher borrowing costs could be a tailwind for Bitcoin.

According to recent reports, "First, you're gonna hike rates. Oh, sell gold, right? You're going to go to the dollar. It's so ingrained in peoples' heads," he said.

"Carry costs going up," he said. Bitcoin doesn't offer the same yield as interest-bearing dollar assets.

"You don't make any interest on Bitcoin in dollars," he mentioned.

In particular, Novogratz noted that the massive rise in Treasury yields has been particularly detrimental to the crypto market.

"Literally 40 basis points in like four days of trading. So that's why crypto's down," he noted.

He also remarked that the massive crypto hack could still be weighing on investors' minds, adding to market jitters.

"I think in the back of their minds is the hack," he said.

When shopping for men’s travel blazers, look for fabrics that are comfy and practical. Men’s travel blazers are built to look like traditional blazers, while providing the feel and function of athletic outerwear. Go for stretchy materials like spandex or elastane, so you can move without any hassle or restriction. Wrinkle-resistant materials like polyester or blends are great because they remain looking sharp after you unravel them from your suitcase. Breathable materials like cotton and lightweight wool keep you cool and comfortable.

It has been revealed that make sure your blazer fits well and is comfortable enough to wear all day. Travel blazers for men should allow freedom of movement and not feel too tight or restrictive. The shoulders of the garment need to align with your own and not sag or pinch, as this affects the overall look. Always double-check the sleeves; see that they’re not too long and the armholes are high enough to avoid bunching while allowing mobility. When it comes to travel blazers, you'll typically find these three main types of fits.

A more tailored cut that's snug around the chest and waist, giving you a sharp, sleek silhouette. Great for guys who want a more fitted look without sacrificing comfort.

A fit that's perfect for guys with broader shoulders and a smaller waist. It offers more room in the chest and shoulders, while still tapering at the waist for a streamlined look.

The classic, relaxed fit. It offers more room throughout the body and is great for a laid-back, comfortable look. Ideal for guys who prioritize freedom of movement and a less structured feel.

Check for practical features like multiple pockets for easy access to essentials and moisture-wicking properties if you intend to be active.

We also analyzed the packing process and styled the blazer with different outfits to make sure it worked for both casual and formal settings. We then narrowed down to the eight best travel blazers for men that give you a stylish and refined look that attracts only the best kind of attention.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am.

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

According to recent reports, the two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA said.

In its latest upgrade on the investigation, ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

Industry observers note that on Tuesday, ULA said early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

Industry observers note that the BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp noted Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the manufacturer looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

In a recent development, the finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own Latest Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn releases reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA said.

Recent findings suggest that the Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA noted it will share more as the investigation continues.

  • We’ve seen this before: Latest technology dramatically lowers the cost of starting and running a business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Just as the Industrial Revolution transformed business through machines, mass production and long-distance transportation, AI may be powering a latest entrepreneurial boom.

We’ve seen this before: Latest technology dramatically lowers the cost of starting and running a business. But where the steam engine and electricity offered only a first step, still requiring substantial capital for machinery, factories and workers, AI offers modern entrepreneurs a full staircase. Today, an aspiring founder with a good idea can access powerful capabilities with little more than a computer and a Wi-Fi connection. The challenge is knowing what you need to launch and grow a business at each stage.

In a recent development, business creation has surged in 2026, with nearly every month setting a record for new registrations compared with the same month in previous years. Since January, 5.9 million new businesses have been formed nationwide — up 16% from the same period in 2025 and 24% from 2024.

In a recent development, what’s driving that growth? It’s not a single engine but a combination of forces, including the continued popularity of remote work and the appeal of being your own boss and having more financial freedom, both now more within reach because of AI.

If you previously dropped a business idea because it seemed too complicated or expensive, now may be the time to reconsider. AI has reached a level of capability that didn’t exist just a few years ago. It’s steadily eroding traditional startup barriers, helping founders turn even ambitious ideas into real businesses with less money, fewer employees and fewer outside resources.

Recent findings suggest that until recently, launching a organization often meant spending money before making money. Office space, equipment, expensive software and employees with specialized skills were requirements in most sectors, not to mention the accountants and consultants needed just to get started.

Sources indicate that now, cloud infrastructure has replaced costly servers. No-code platforms make it possible to build websites and apps without extensive programming knowledge. E-commerce platforms give small companies access to national and global markets. Generative AI accelerates this trend by helping entrepreneurs research markets, analyze competitors, draft business plans, develop marketing campaigns, create content and automate tedious administrative work.

Sources indicate that start by asking yourself, “What do I need to reach customers at this stage, and how will it maximize my return on investment?” Use inexpensive tools to create a product prototype, a landing page or a basic marketing campaign. Talk to potential customers. Test your pricing and measure the response. Save major investments for ideas that show real demand.

In a recent development, AI gives founders a chance to rethink hiring. Entrepreneurs once had to hire employees or contractors before they were generating enough revenue to support them. Today, a solo founder with the right AI tools can handle many of those functions alone.

Industry observers note that that doesn’t mean putting complete trust in a chatbot. AI-assisted work still requires human oversight, judgment, verification and refinement. And when you’re building a trustworthy brand from scratch, you have to consider accuracy, privacy and legal concerns.

Use AI to draft routine marketing emails, but hire an experienced marketer when strategy matters. Organize basic finances with bookkeeping software, but consult an accountant for crucial tax decisions. Automate answers to repetitive customer service questions, but keep a human in the loop for complicated interactions or when customers ask for one. The goal isn’t to eliminate employees. It’s to delay fixed expenses until your business can support them.

Historically, founders moved to places like San Francisco or Austin because those cities offered concentrated pools of money and talent. Those hubs remain vibrant, but AI and remote technology are reducing the importance of location.

A tech founder in a small town can use the same AI platforms and cloud services as someone in Silicon Valley. Remote collaboration provides access to talent anywhere, and e-commerce can reach customers far beyond a firm’s hometown.

With AI tools, you can explore many ideas from almost anywhere. Instead of asking, “Where does my business need to be based?” you can ask, “Where would I like to live while I grow my business?” That kind of freedom can make a real difference in your quality of life.

Forming a business and building a successful one are different things. Many of the companies registered this year will never become fully operational. Others will struggle to find customers or stay profitable. AI can’t fix a weak business model, create demand where none exists or eliminate the financial risks of entrepreneurship.

What AI can do is make the process easier and cheaper, and therein lies the lesson. Instead of investing heavily up front in one untested concept, make a series of small bets. Develop a minimum viable product. Test marketing messages. Experiment with prices. Ask AI to identify the assumptions in your business strategy, then test them with real customers and real-world data.

With more than 5 million businesses formed since the start of 2026, the U.S. could finish the year with close to 7 million new registrations if the current pace continues. There’s evidence that AI may be contributing to that momentum. But like the steam engine, electricity, the internet and smartphones before it, AI is a tool. The real power lies with entrepreneurs who are willing to start lean, test early, automate selectively and spend strategically. With that approach, we may see a boom not only in startups with potential but, more importantly, in businesses that endure.
